Un equipo francés grabó en directo a los saeteros de Jerez, Arcos y Lebrija en la Semana Santa de 1993 para la colección Flamenco vivo.

scenes.name: Demófilo y los Machado
scenes.desc: Antonio Machado y Álvarez, Demófilo, fue el primer autor español que dedicó un libro entero al flamenco: la Colección de cantes flamencos recogidos y anotados (1881), piedra angular de la flamencología moderna; escribió también sobre las saetas y dirigió la revista El Folclore Andaluz (1882-1883). Sus hijos, los poetas Antonio y Manuel Machado (autor de Cante hondo), heredaron la afición, y sus coplas se cantan a menudo sin que los cantaores sepan que son versos cultos. Calixto Sánchez dedicó a Antonio Machado un disco en 2001, y José Menese hizo suyas las letras de Francisco Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: La farruca y el garrotín
scenes.desc: Cantes aflamencados de fuera de Andalucía. La farruca, gallega, llegó a Cádiz con los comerciantes gallegos del XIX y es más baile que cante; la popularizó Manuel Torre a principios del XX y hoy casi solo la canta Pepe Menese, con una letra de Moreno Galván que se hizo himno en la Transición. Su baile, viril, lo creó Faíco; Carmen Amaya lo bailó vestida de hombre, Falla lo incluyó en El sombrero de tres picos y la versión de Antonio Gades en la película de Los Tarantos, la última de Carmen Amaya, se enseña hoy en las academias. El garrotín viene del folclore asturiano y lo hicieron suyo los gitanos de Lleida; lo difundieron Carmen Amaya y la Niña de los Peines, que lo cantaba con aire de tangos, Faíco hizo sus coreografías y Blas Vega recogió una copla antigua cantada por el Chaparro en la Magna antología del cante flamenco.

scenes.name: Los maestros antiguos del toque
scenes.desc: La guitarra pasó en los cafés cantantes a ocupar el lugar de panderetas y bandurrias, pero hasta mediados del siglo XX el tocaor vivía escondido detrás del cantaor. El Maestro Patiño (1829-1902), gran maestro del siglo XIX, introdujo la cejilla para adaptarse al tono de cada cantaor. Javier Molina (1868-1956) fundó la escuela jerezana y conservó la pureza del acompañamiento. Miguel Borrull fue el gran acompañante de los cantes de Levante y uno de los preferidos de Chacón. Ramón Montoya (1879-1949), tocaor fijo de Chacón entre 1912 y 1926, fue el primer renovador del acompañamiento y difundió la guitarra flamenca por el mundo. Perico el del Lunar acompañó a Chacón y dirigió la antología de 1954 que abrió la revalorización. El Niño Ricardo (1904-1972), la bisagra entre el toque antiguo y el moderno, era el más solicitado por los cantaores e ídolo de juventud de Paco de Lucía. Diego del Gastor (1908-1973) creó la escuela de Morón en la intimidad, sin profesionalizarse nunca, y tiene discípulos en Estados Unidos y Japón.

scenes.name: Los fandangos de Huelva
scenes.desc: Huelva reclama la cuna del fandango andaluz y es la provincia con más estilos: las antologías recogen más de treinta y cinco, locales (Encinasola, el Alosno, Cabezas Rubias, Calañas, el Andévalo, Valverde del Camino) y personales, creados por profesionales como Paco Isidro, Pepe Rebollo, el Comía, Antonio Rengel, Pérez de Guzmán y Paco Toronjo; de fuera dejaron su sello el Gloria, Macandé, el Carbonerillo y Manolo Caracol. Paco Toronjo, fijo en los festivales desde finales de los sesenta y en las bienales de Sevilla, les dio una jondura difícil de imitar. El baile, de pareja y galanteo, se ve ya poco.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Levante o de las minas
scenes.desc: Nacidos del trabajo en las minas del siglo XIX en las sierras de Cartagena y La Unión y en Linares, La Carolina y Andújar: cantes de dolor profundo sobre la mina, sus accidentes y los compañeros muertos, hechos con fandangos regionales, murcianas, malagueñas y el cante de madrugá de los mineros. La taranta, el más significativo, tiene dos estilos, el de Linares (Gabriel Moreno, Carmen Linares) y el de La Unión (Encarnación Fernández, Pepe Cros), y Camarón le puso dulzura; el taranto, almeriense, tiene compás porque nació para el baile de Carmen Amaya en los cuarenta, con el Ciego de la Playa y Pedro el Morato. La cartagenera, de temas más urbanos, la fijó Antonio Chacón a finales del XIX y la cantaron Cayetano Muriel, Manuel Centeno, Manuel Torre y la Niña de los Peines. La minera se atribuye a Rojo el Alpargatero, Antonio Grau Mora, que hacia 1885 abrió en La Unión una posada que acabó en café cantante y oía cantar a los mineros de madrugada: es el gran creador de los cantes mineros. Las granaínas, de Frasquito Yerbabuena y sobre todo Chacón, son un cante casi barroco hoy cargado de vibratos operísticos. Sin minas, los concursos de Linares y La Unión mantienen vivos estos cantes.

scenes.name: Las cantiñas: alegrías, caracoles, mirabrás y romeras
scenes.desc: Cantes alegres de la bahía de Cádiz, en compás de soleá y muy ligados al baile, que arranca majestuoso y va ganando fuerza hasta desplantes electrizantes. Nacen probablemente de la jotilla gaditana, hermanada con la jota aragonesa por la resistencia común contra Napoleón, de ahí las letras sobre la guerra y el mar; la leyenda atribuye su creación a Enrique el Mellizo, que oyó a una muchacha cantar jotas con un ciego. Tomaron identidad en la segunda mitad del XIX. Hay cantiñas del Pinini de Utrera y Lebrija y de Córdoba; la rosa ya no se canta. Las alegrías, al principio baile de mujer sola, se hicieron más lentas a comienzos del XX y empiezan con el «tirititrán» que, según Chano Lobato, inventó Pericón de Cádiz al olvidar la letra; las cantaron el Mellizo, Ignacio Ezpeleta, Aurelio Sellés, Manolo Vargas y Pericón. Los caracoles, de Tío José el Granaíno (picador del Chiclanero), los recreó Chacón y triunfaron en Madrid («la gran calle de Alcalá»). El mirabrás son alegrías largas (José Menese, con letras de Moreno Galván), y las romeras se atribuyen al Granaíno o a una cantaora llamada la Romera. Hoy el gran intérprete es Chano Lobato.

scenes.name: Los tangos, tientos y marianas
scenes.desc: Con bulerías y cantiñas, el gran cante festero: letras de vida, amor y muerte con cierta ligereza, ritmo vivo y pegadizo fácil de seguir con palmas, y un baile sensual. Cádiz y Sevilla se disputan su paternidad, pero los hay en toda Andalucía y en Extremadura; Triana tiene el estilo del Titi y Jerez su propio sello. Su origen musical se discute: Mairena los tenía por cante básico gitano; los estudios recientes los llevan a Cuba y las habaneras llegadas a Sevilla y Cádiz en la segunda mitad del XIX; los granadinos defienden una raíz morisca (el disco Granada canta por tangos recoge trece estilos, entre ellos los de la morería). Manuel Ríos Ruiz concluye que no se sabe con certeza. La Niña de los Peines se hizo inmortal con su copla «Péinate tú con mis peines». Del tango nacen los tientos, más pausados y solemnes, que cantaron primero el Mellizo y el Marrurro y se popularizaron a comienzos del XX, y la mariana, que difundió Bernardo el de los Lobitos y hoy casi solo canta Pepe Menese con letras de Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: Las soleares
scenes.desc: La madre del cante y uno de sus pilares, independiente de cualquier otro ritmo; los cantaores la consideran «el toro bravo del arte jondo». Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los romances
scenes.desc: El flamenco distingue una docena de palos (romances, tonás, siguiriyas, soleares, tangos, cantiñas, cantes de Levante, fandangos, cantes de Málaga, ida y vuelta, aflamencados e híbridos), cada uno con sus estilos y sus creadores. Los básicos, los más antiguos, empiezan por el romance, la canción española más vieja transmitida oralmente, que los gitanos hicieron suya: es el verdadero punto de origen del cante. También llamados corridos, son las únicas coplas con continuidad narrativa (historias románticas, caballerescas o moriscas) y se cantan a palo seco, sin acompañamiento; con guitarra toman el son de la soleá por bulerías. Washington Irving los oyó en 1829 como «tonadas rudas y sencillas». Hoy casi no se cantan. José Blas Vega grabó en 1971 en el Puerto de Santa María dieciséis romances primitivos de siete intérpretes, todos gitanos, y los dividió en los de flores y Blancaflor, los carolingios, los del Cid, los de Bernardo el Carpio y los moriscos, como el de Zaide; su parentesco con tonás, carceleras, deblas y martinetes es evidente.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Early Musical Exposure (1959)
facts.body: Robert Zimmerman, later known as Bob Dylan, saw one of the "Winter Dance Party" shows in Duluth, Minnesota, where Buddy Holly, Dion, and Richie Valens were filling in on drums. This early experience occurred before Zimmerman moved to Greenwich Village. "The shows were still good, at least according to a young man named Robert Zimmerman, who saw the first drummers show in Duluth, Minnesota."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Bob Dylan

facts.title: Plane Crash Death (1959)
facts.body: Buddy Holly was killed in a small plane crash in a cornfield outside Mason City, Iowa, on February 3, 1959. This tragedy, which also claimed the lives of Ritchie Valens and Big Wopper, is historically referred to as "the day the music died." "Buddy Holly, Richie Val, and Big Wopper were all killed when their small plane went down in a cornfield outside of Mason City, Iowa."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Airplanes!
facts.name: Buddy Holly

facts.title: The Winter Dance Party Tour Conditions (1959)
facts.body: The tour in Wisconsin, Iowa, and Minnesota through January and February 1959 was plagued by miserable conditions, including zigzagging routes with 400-mile distances between gigs, musicians sleeping on buses, and using eight different buses in 11 days due to breakdowns. Heating failures in temperatures as low as minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit and three feet of snow caused illness (flu for Bopper and Valens) and frostbite (Carl Bunch). "The musicians had to sleep on the tour bus, or buses."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: A young man named Robert Zimmerman, later known as Bob Dylan, saw one of the Winter Dance Party shows in Duluth, Minnesota, where Holly, Dion, and Valens were taking turns playing drums due to their drummer's frostbite. "The shows were still good, at least according to a young man named Robert Zimmerman, who saw the first drummers show in Duluth, Minnesota."

facts.title: Plane Crash Circumstances (1959)
facts.body: After a show in Clear Lake, Iowa, Holly chartered a plane to Fargo, North Dakota, to get laundry done and sleep in a real bed. Tommy Allsup and Waylon Jennings gave up their seats to the Big Bopper and Richie Valens, who were suffering the most from the tour conditions. The pilot, despite being good in daylight, had a poor instrument flight rating, and the plane had an unusual altimeter that functioned inversely to typical models. The plane plummeted nose first less than five minutes after takeoff, killing everyone instantly. "The plane took off, and less than five minutes after takeoff, it plummeted straight down, nose first, into the ground top speed, killing everyone on board instantly."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Maria Elena's Tragic Discovery and Miscarriage (1959)
facts.body: Maria Elena learned of Buddy Holly's death from the television, not the police, which later prompted changes in how news of celebrity deaths was handled. She was so distraught that she miscarried two days later and has never been able to visit his grave. "Maria Elena found out about Bodies Death, not from the police, but from the TV."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Posthumous Financial Success for Petty (1959-1965)
facts.body: After Holly's death, Norman Petty profited immensely from a stockpile of unreleased Buddy Holly recordings. He also secured an agreement with Holly's estate to overdub new backing tracks onto Holly's acoustic demos, transforming them into full-band rock and roll songs, which resulted in posthumous hit singles until 1965 outside the US, making both Petty and Holly's estate wealthy. "Suddenly, his stockpile of unreleased Buddy Holly recordings was a gold mine, and not only that, he ended up coming to an agreement with Holly's estate that he could take all those demos Holly had recorded, and overdub new backing tracks on them, turning them into full-blown rock-and-roll songs."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: "Go Johnny Go" Film Appearance (1959)
facts.body: Chuck Berry co-starred as himself with Alan Fried in the 1959 film "Go Johnny Go," which took its title from Berry's hit song. The movie proved to be a final moment of rock and roll cultural relevance for many involved, as several featured artists faced professional decline or untimely deaths shortly after its release. "That film came out in 1959 and had Barry as Fried's co-star, appearing with Fried as himself in almost every scene."

facts.body: By mid-1959, Roy Orbison was considered an "absolute failure" despite being produced by notable figures like Sam Phillips and Chet Atkins. facts.title: Conspicuous Presence at First Grammys (1959)
facts.body: Frank Sinatra was the "most conspicuous presence" at the first Grammy Awards ceremony held in May 1959 at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, where he notably bought two tables for his Rat Pack friends. Despite high expectations, being nominated for five Grammys, he left with only an album packaging award. "Cruelling legend Frank Sinatra was the most conspicuous presence. He'd bought two tables for his rat-packed friends."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.name: Frank Sinatra

facts.title: Grammy Snub at First Ceremony (1959)
facts.body: Despite being nominated for five Grammys, including two for Album of the Year and Record of the Year for "Witchcraft," Frank Sinatra "came away with almost nothing" at the inaugural Grammys in 1959, winning only an album packaging award and no performance Grammys. He was reportedly "furious." "But that night, Sinatra came away with almost nothing, winning only an album packaging award for his LP Only The Lonely, and not a single performance Grammy."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.body: Frank Sinatra was the "most conspicuous presence" at the first Grammy Awards ceremony held in May 1959 at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, where he notably bought two tables for his Rat Pack friends. Despite high expectations, being nominated for five Grammys, he left with only an album packaging award. "Cruelling legend Frank Sinatra was the most conspicuous presence. He'd bought two tables for his rat-packed friends."

facts.title: Grammy Snub at First Ceremony (1959)
facts.body: Despite being nominated for five Grammys, including two for Album of the Year and Record of the Year for "Witchcraft," Frank Sinatra "came away with almost nothing" at the inaugural Grammys in 1959, winning only an album packaging award and no performance Grammys. He was reportedly "furious." "But that night, Sinatra came away with almost nothing, winning only an album packaging award for his LP Only The Lonely, and not a single performance Grammy."

facts.title: Founding (July 4, 1959)
facts.body: Island Records was founded on July 4th, 1959, by Englishman Chris Blackwell and two partners in Jamaica. The label's name was inspired by the Harry Belafonte song "Island in the Sun," and it began with a startup capital of 100 pounds. "So on July 4th, 1959, he and two partners created Island Records, taking the name from the Harry Belafonte song Island in the Sun."

facts.title: Founding and Early Support (1959)
facts.body: Founded in 1959 by Chris Blackwell, a wealthy Brit who grew up in Jamaica, Island Records was sustained in its early, less profitable years by considerable financial backing from Blackwell's parents. "Chris Blackwell, a wealthy white guy who started his own record label, Island Records in 1959. Blackwell is a Brit who grew up in Jamaica, and with quite a bit of financial support from Mom and Dad, was able to keep Island records afloat when it wasn't bringing in too much money."

facts.body: Ritchie Valens was killed in a small plane crash in a cornfield outside Mason City, Iowa, on February 3, 1959. facts.title: Death in Plane Crash (1959)
facts.body: Richie Valens died in a plane crash on February 3, 1959, along with Buddy Holly and The Big Bopper, while traveling during the "Winter Dance Party" tour. facts.body: The Marshall stack, officially known as the Marshall Super Lead Model 1959, became the foundational design for the "walls of Marshall amps and cabinets" seen today. Available in half-stack (one cabinet) or full-stack (two cabinets driven by a head) configurations, it is considered the most iconic amp setup for guitarists seeking volume, power, and distortion. "This was the Marshall stack, officially known as the Marshall Super Lead Model 1959. It is the basis for all the walls of Marshall amps and cabinets that we see today, either with a half-stack design with one speaker cabinet or a full stack with a head unit driving two cabinets."

facts.body: The chain's first flagship store opened at 259 Yonge Street in 1959. It later relocated to a more expansive site at 347 Yonge Street in 1961, which became a cultural landmark in Toronto. facts.body: Originating from extended, improvised call-and-response endings to their live performances of Jackie Wilson's "Lonely Teardrops," this song gradually developed with elements from Roquel's records like "What Did I Say" and "I Got A Woman." Producers Hugo and Luigi suggested cutting out the "Lonely Teardrops" part and recording just the extended tag. The resulting song, split into "Shout Parts One and Two" across a single, became the Isley Brothers' first chart hit, reaching number 47. Credited to the three brothers, it generated significant income from numerous successful cover versions, and sold over a million copies despite not breaking the Top 40. "That was nothing like anything that Hugo and Luigi had ever produced before, and it became the Isle Brothers' first chart hit, reaching number 47."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Credited as a solo composition by Valens, this song is noted for its resemblance to Little Richard's "Ooh! My Soul," suggesting it originated from Valens performing and then creatively altering another artist's material until it became distinct. Led Zeppelin later employed a similar creative process with "Ooh My Head" to produce "Boogie with Stu." Bob Keane, holding the publishing rights for Valens' songs, successfully sued Led Zeppelin for this, despite their attempt to preempt a lawsuit by crediting Valens' mother as a co-writer. Valens performed "Ooh My Head" in the Alan Freed film "Go Johnny Go." "Valence's song seems to have come from precisely this process, of performing someone else's song, and changing it around until it became something different."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Initially released in early 1959 as the B-side of the ballad "Teardrops on Your Letter," this song reached number 16 on the R&B chart. It was recorded in late 1958 and stemmed from a 15-bar blues song by the Sensational Nightingales, which Ballard and guitarist Cal Green adapted to a pre-existing 12-bar melody previously used on their song "Is Your Love For Real." This melody had a long ancestry, inspired by Clyde McPhatter and The Drifters and showing influence from The Radio 4. Initially, it featured a Jimmy Reed-style blues beat, which was changed for the studio recording in November 1958 with a new intro. An earlier demo for VJ Records reportedly contained sexually suggestive lyrics from the Nightingales' original. Ballard was credited as the sole writer, omitting the Nightingales, Green, and other contributing songwriters. Years later, King Records overdubbed an identical saxophone part onto Ballard's track and reissued it to make it sound more like Chubby Checker's successful version, which led to Ballard's version reaching number 28 on the pop charts. "It was released with Ballard as the sole credited writer as the base side of a ballad called Teardrops on Your Letter."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Emil Ford and the Checkmates released a "sound-like cover version" of an oldie from 1916 that Johnny Otis had previously attempted to revive. While Otis's version failed commercially, Ford's cover became the last British number one hit of the 1950s and the first of the 1960s. This record also achieved two significant milestones: it was the first number one hit by a black British artist and the first record by a black British person to sell over a million copies. Joe Meek was a co-producer on this record. "Sadly, it sank without a trace, at least until it was picked up by Emil Ford and the checkmates, who released a sound-like cover version, which became the last British number one of the 50s and first of the 60s, and was also the first number one hit by a black British artist, and the first record by a black British person to sell them all in copies."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

His backing band, The Shadows, devised a synchronized dance routine to enhance the visual presentation of the song during live performances. The positive audience reaction to this specific routine led The Shadows to incorporate unison movement into all their songs, giving rise to their signature "Shadows' Walk." "Cliff Richard caught his own version of William the Han Jive in 1959."

facts.title: Fundación por Daphne Oram (1959)
facts.body: Fundado por Daphne Oram en 1959, Oramics Studios for electronic music and composition fue el primer estudio de música electrónica creado por una mujer. Oram estableció este estudio tras abandonar el BBC Radiofonic Workshop para centrarse en su innovadora técnica Oramics, que implicaba dibujar directamente sobre película de 35 milímetros para generar sonidos. "El primer estudio de música electrónica creado por una mujer."

facts.title: Plane Crash Death (1959)
facts.body: Big Wopper was killed in a small plane crash in a cornfield outside Mason City, Iowa, on February 3, 1959. This tragedy, which also claimed the lives of Buddy Holly and Ritchie Valens, is historically referred to as "the day the music died." "Buddy Holly, Richie Val, and Big Wopper were all killed when their small plane went down in a cornfield outside of Mason City, Iowa."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Airplanes!
facts.name: Big Wopper

facts.title: Avro Arrow Project Cancellation (1959)
facts.body: The Canadian government canceled the Avro Arrow, a state-of-the-art jet fighter developed in the 1950s and considered one of the greatest air machines, on February 20th, 1959. This decision resulted in 50,000 people losing their jobs. However, many of the project's engineers were subsequently hired by the newly formed American organization NASA, becoming integral to the Apollo space program, or found work in Britain and France contributing to the development of Concorde. The cancellation is cited as an example of a "hinge factor," where a seemingly negative event had unforeseen, significant impacts on future projects. "So really, who knows if these two projects would have ever succeeded as well as they did had Prime Minister Diefenbiker not canceled the Avro Arrow?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

facts.title: The Day the Music Died (1959)
facts.body: The infamous event known as "The Day the Music Died" occurred in 1959, claiming the lives of Buddy Holly, The Big Bopper, and Ritchie Valens. Their chartered single-engine aircraft crashed in an Iowa cornfield, a tragedy that left a profound mark on music history. "There was the infamous The Day the Music died in 1959 that saw Buddy Holly, the big bopper and Richie Valens die when their chartered single engine aircraft went down in an Iowa cornfield."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing...Uncharted: The Lynyrd Skynyrd Plane Crash

facts.title: Invention by John Koss (1959)
facts.body: In the mid-1950s, John Koss, while trying to promote his portable record player, engineered a set of headphones as an afterthought to demonstrate the device privately. Although his record player failed, the headphones proved to be a "brilliant idea." In 1959, the first Koss headphones were introduced, initiating the widespread "headphone craze." `"As an afterthoughts, a way to demonstrate the device, he engineered a set of headphones so people could listen privately. His record player was a bust, but the headphones? That was a brilliant idea, and in 1959, the first ever Koss headphones were introduced, and that was the beginning of the headphone craze."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

facts.body: The next major development in stereo formats was the introduction of the Stereo 7-inch single, which first appeared in May 1959. This brought stereo to the popular single format, further accelerating its market penetration. "The next development came with the Stereo 7-inch single, they first appeared in May 1959."

facts.title: Introduction (May 1959)
facts.body: Stereo 7-inch singles first emerged in May 1959, bringing the new two-channel audio format to the popular single record market. This development contributed significantly to the rapid obsolescence of the older 78 RPM singles. "The next development came with the Stereo 7-inch single, they first appeared in May 1959."

facts.episode: The Story of Stereo: Part 1

facts.title: 30-Watt Output and 1959 Introduction
facts.body: The Vox AC30 is a 30-watt amplifier model first introduced in 1959. Its release marked a significant departure from the predominantly American-made amplifiers used by most electric guitarists at the time, which had resulted in a more uniform guitar tone across the industry. "The most important model was the 30-watt Vox AC30, first introduced in 1959. Until Vox came along, the majority of electric guitars were using amps built by Fender and a few other small American manufacturers."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

facts.title: Initial Category Exclusions (1959)
facts.body: At the first Grammys, major genres such as rock and roll were conspicuously absent from award categories, while jazz, classical, pop, country, Broadway, movie soundtracks, comedy, and children's music all had dedicated awards. Only one category was created for R&B. "At the first Grammys, held in May 1959 in a ballroom at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, complete with a catered dinner."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: And the Grammy Goes to… Edition Part 1

facts.title: Tragic Tour Conditions (1959)
facts.body: The "Winter Dance Party" tour, spanning Wisconsin, Iowa, and Minnesota in early 1959, was marked by miserable logistical and environmental conditions, including a zigzagging route with gigs up to 400 miles apart, constant bus breakdowns (eight buses in 11 days), non-functioning heating in sub-zero temperatures (minus 40 Fahrenheit) with three feet of snow, leading to illness (flu for Big Bopper, Valens) and frostbite (Carl Bunch). "The Winter Dance Party toured Wisconsin, Iowa and Minnesota through the end of January and the beginning of February 1959, and the conditions were miserable for everyone concerned."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

facts.title: Reduced Lineup and Financial Woes (1959)
facts.body: The tour had a surprisingly small lineup of only five acts (Frankie Sado, Dion and The Belmonts, The Big Bopper, Richie Valens, Buddy Holly), and was run on a shoestring budget. After the fatal plane crash, the remaining performers were forced to continue the 13 remaining dates without the headliners and were not paid their full wages due to the bill being unadvertised. "This one had only five. There was an opening act called Frankie Sado, and then Dion and the Belmont, who had had a few minor hits, and had just recorded, but not yet released."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

facts.title: Altitude Meter Anomaly (1959)
facts.body: The plane involved in the fatal crash had an unusual altitude meter where the needle went down when the plane was going up, and up when the plane was going down, contributing to pilot error in instrument flight conditions. "that particular model's meter went down when the plane was going up, and up when the plane was going down."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

facts.title: Changes in Celebrity Death Announcements (Post-1959)
facts.body: Maria Elena Santiago learning of Buddy Holly's death from the television, rather than official notification, prompted later changes in how news of celebrity deaths was to be revealed to family members. "This later prompted changes in how news of celebrity deaths was to be revealed."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

facts.title: The Shadows' Walk (1959)
facts.body: This distinctive synchronized dance routine was developed by Cliff Richard's backing band, The Shadows. It originated during a live performance of Richard's cover of "Willie and the Hand Jive," where the band sought to enhance the visual presentation of the song. The audience's enthusiastic response led The Shadows to adopt these unison movements for all their subsequent performances, solidifying it as their signature stage presence. "The audience reaction was so great that they started doing it on every song, the famous or infamous Shadows' work had developed."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
